title: MacWhisper vs VoiceInk on Mac in 2026: prices, privacy and which one to pick
metaTitle: MacWhisper vs VoiceInk on Mac: prices, privacy and which to pick
description: MacWhisper vs VoiceInk compared on price, privacy, file transcription and dictation on Mac. See where each app wins and who should pick which.
intro: MacWhisper fits better if your work starts with recordings and files. VoiceInk fits better if you mostly dictate text and want to read the code yourself. Both are Mac-only apps that stress local processing, but they charge differently, so compare the checkout prices before you buy. Lazur is a different kind of tool, and it appears here as a third option for context.
tldr: MacWhisper is the better pick for audio and video files, subtitle exports and 100 languages, according to its own site.
VoiceInk is the better pick for dictation, public code and one-time licenses that cover up to three Macs.
Both apps promote local processing. MacWhisper keeps cloud AI optional, and VoiceInk's cloud enhancement is also opt-in.
The prices use different currencies, €64 for MacWhisper Pro and $25 to $49 for VoiceInk, so compare checkout totals.
Lazur is a voice assistant that answers questions about your screen. File transcription is not one of its listed features.

blocks.text: MacWhisper vs VoiceInk: what each app is built for

Both apps turn speech into text on your Mac, and both sell one-time licenses. The jobs they do best are different. MacWhisper is built around recordings and files. VoiceInk is built around dictation, and its homepage stresses local processing and public code.

MacWhisper's site lists the features you would expect from a file tool. It records from your Mac microphone, imports audio and video files, and transcribes media from a URL. It supports 100 languages and exports to .srt, .vtt, .txt, .md, .pdf, .html and .docx. It also offers automatic speaker recognition, batch transcription, translation and meeting auto-recording. It can run local models through Ollama and LM Studio.

VoiceInk's homepage says it processes all voice transcription locally on your device. It says your voice data never leaves your Mac. It also says the project is built in public on GitHub, so you can read or run every line. It requires Apple silicon and macOS 14.4 or later, and it recommends 8GB of RAM. Those are the vendor's claims. Check the public repository yourself if code access matters to you.
Where MacWhisper is the better pick

items: You transcribe interviews, lectures or video often. Batch transcription and media URL import are built for that kind of work.
You need subtitles or Word files. MacWhisper exports .srt, .vtt and .docx among its formats.
You want speaker labels in a transcript. The vendor lists automatic speaker recognition.
You work in a language other than English. MacWhisper lists 100 languages.
You want to try the app before you pay. The free tier is listed as free forever.

blocks.text: Where VoiceInk is the better pick

items: You mostly dictate and want the default processing to stay on your Mac.
You want to read the code before you trust it. VoiceInk says every line is public on GitHub.
You own more than one Mac. Personal covers two Macs, and Extended covers three.
You want a refund window. VoiceInk offers a 14-day money-back guarantee, no questions asked.
You want updates included. VoiceInk says its license includes future updates.

blocks.text: MacWhisper vs VoiceInk price: how the licenses compare

MacWhisper's site lists a Free tier at €0, free forever, and a Pro tier at a one-time €64 per license. The page says Pro includes lifetime updates. Third-party reviews quote other figures and other currencies. Treat those as unverified until you see the checkout page.

VoiceInk prices its licenses in dollars on its pricing page. Solo is $25 for one Mac. Personal is $39 for up to two Macs, and the page marks it best value. Extended is $49 for up to three Macs. Each one is a one-time payment with no subscription, and the page offers a 14-day money-back guarantee.

Here is a worked example. Say you have a work Mac and a home Mac. Personal at $39 covers both. Two Solo licenses would cost more than that single Personal license, and they would still be two separate purchases. The point is to match the tier to the number of Macs you actually use.

Mind the currency. MacWhisper's site shows euros, and VoiceInk's pricing page shows dollars. Do not treat €64 and $39 as the same unit. Open both checkout pages, then compare the totals in one currency. Add any local tax the checkout shows, so the numbers match what you will pay.

Subscriptions change the math. Lazur sells monthly plans, not a one-time license. Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Power is $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, with 1,000 AI actions. Both Mac apps in this comparison charge once for a paid license, so a monthly bill is a different kind of cost.
MacWhisper vs VoiceInk privacy: where your voice and files go

MacWhisper says it uses local models to transcribe your files. It calls that approach perfect for your most sensitive and private files. The site says you can process sensitive content locally, with no data leaving your Mac. Cloud AI is optional. The page does not say where data goes when you turn cloud AI on. Ask the vendor before you send client or medical recordings through cloud AI.

VoiceInk makes a narrower promise. Its homepage says all voice transcription runs on your device. Its FAQ says cloud enhancement is optional, and it processes only the transcribed text if you turn it on, not your voice. Text still leaves your Mac when that setting is on, so treat it as a choice you make, not a default you can forget.

Read the settings, not only the homepage. A reviewer who logged 2,794 dictations over several months wrote, 'Local isn't automatic.' That is one person's log, not a survey, but it matches the FAQ. Check the cloud option in VoiceInk's settings, then check it again after each update.

MakerStack's MacWhisper review gave the app 7.3 out of 10. The reviewer called its privacy guarantee absolute and praised the lifetime value. The same review criticises the Mac-only lock-in and the lack of real-time app dictation. MakerStack discloses sponsor placement fees, so weigh the score with that in mind.
Dictation on Mac: speed, errors and what to test

Dictation is where most people start. A 2016 arXiv study by Ruan and colleagues measured English speech input at 153 words per minute. Keyboard entry measured 52 words per minute, a ratio of 2.93. The participants entered short phrases on phones, so the test does not prove that long documents will be faster. Speech also left more uncorrected errors, at 1.30% of the final text against 0.79% for keyboard.

The study gives you a simple rule for either app. Speech is faster, but it needs a read-through before you send anything. Check names, numbers and punctuation first. Those are the spots where errors tend to hide. Fixing them takes minutes, which is still less time than typing the whole draft by hand.

Dictation features also differ. MacWhisper's site lists system-wide dictation, and a TodayOnMac article says Global mode requires Pro. VoiceInk's homepage describes on-device voice transcription, and a reviewer reported a median wait of 0.71 seconds across one log. Test both in the apps you use every day, since speed depends on your Mac, your model and your microphone.

If dictation returns nothing, open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and confirm the app has access. Then hold the shortcut again and speak for a few seconds before you judge the result. Many failed tests are really permission problems.
Transcribing audio and video files on a Mac

This is the clearest gap between the two apps. MacWhisper is built for files. You import an audio or video file, or paste a media URL, then export the transcript in the format you need. For a folder of recordings, batch transcription saves time. A third-party article says batch jobs need Pro, so check the current license terms before you plan a large project.

VoiceInk's pages do not list file import or export formats. Its pages focus on voice on your device, so do not assume it handles a folder of video files. Check its site or ask the developer before you buy. If file transcription is your main job, that gap probably decides the choice.

Watch for formats and speakers. If your output must be an .srt file for video editing, MacWhisper lists that export. If you need speaker labels for a panel recording, MacWhisper lists automatic speaker recognition. Neither feature appears on the VoiceInk pages checked for this comparison, so test them before you rely on them.
How to test both apps before you pay

items: Pick a short recording with more than one speaker and a few names in it.
Open MacWhisper's free tier and transcribe the file. Note which models the free tier offers, since a third-party article says it covers the smaller ones.
Turn on speaker recognition and check whether the labels match the speakers.
Dictate the same passage into a document in VoiceInk, using its free trial button.
Count the words you have to fix by hand in each result. That count matters more than the speed claim.

blocks.text: Keep the test honest. Use the same microphone and the same room for both. Read each result against the original audio, not against memory. Write down the number of errors and the minutes it took to fix them. Those notes are worth more than any review score.
Device limits and the mistakes people make

VoiceInk's license tiers depend on how many Macs you use. Solo covers one Mac, Personal covers up to two, and Extended covers up to three. MacWhisper's device count per Pro license was not confirmed on the vendor pages checked, so do not assume a license covers a second Mac until the vendor says so.

items: Comparing €64 with $39 as if they were one currency. Compare checkout totals in one currency.
Assuming local means local. Check cloud settings in each app and turn off anything you do not need.
Buying one Solo license for two Macs. Personal covers two, and Extended covers three.
Trusting third-party prices. Reviews quote different MacWhisper figures, so check the seller page.
Testing with a single short sentence. Short tests can hide errors that appear in longer recordings.

blocks.text: Version matters too. MacWhisper 11 arrived as a free update on 6 December 2024, with a redesigned sidebar and a menu-bar-only mode. Check the version in the app before you compare features, because feature lists change between releases.
Quick scenarios to match the choice

A student recording lectures should start with MacWhisper. Import each lecture, export a .txt or .md file, and search it later. The free tier is enough to test the workflow before you consider a Pro license.
A freelancer dictating client emails should test VoiceInk first. Dictate a real draft, check the names and numbers, and use the 14-day window to decide. Keep cloud enhancement off for client work.

A researcher with interview audio should use MacWhisper for the transcripts and check speaker labels closely. If the same researcher also dictates notes, VoiceInk becomes a second tool. Using both apps is possible, but compare the total cost in one currency before you buy both.
Where Lazur fits in this comparison

Lazur is a different kind of tool, so this is not a like-for-like comparison. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ (Option + Command) to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around it.

Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It also handles everyday voice tasks, such as timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music, opening apps and web search. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is included, but it is not the headline.

Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you, and it is not a plugin for any app. Research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and come back with a summary and a report. Audio and the screenshot are sent to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

Read the [Lazur vs MacWhisper comparison](/compare/lazur-vs-macwhisper) if file transcription is your question. Read the [Lazur vs VoiceInk comparison](/compare/lazur-vs-voiceink) if dictation is. The short version is that Lazur answers questions and guides you through apps, while MacWhisper and VoiceInk turn speech into text.
Which one to pick

Pick MacWhisper if your work starts with recordings and files. It covers import, batch jobs, subtitle and Word exports, speaker labels and 100 languages. Start on the free tier, then decide whether Pro is worth €64 for your workload.

Pick VoiceInk if your work is mostly dictation and you want to read the code. It suits people with up to three Macs who want one-time licenses. Use the 14-day money-back window on real work, so you find out about accuracy and speed in your own apps.
Pick Lazur only if you want a voice helper that sees your screen and talks back. It is a separate category from both apps. Lazur has no partnership with either app maker.
What to do next

items: Open the MacWhisper and VoiceInk checkout pages and compare the totals in one currency.
Turn off cloud options in each app if the files or dictation are private.
Run a short test on a recording you already know well.
Measure your own dictation accuracy with the [dictation accuracy checker](/tools/dictation-accuracy-checker).
Estimate your speaking speed with the [speaking versus typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test).
Check Lazur's [plans and trial](/pricing) if you want a voice helper as well.

blocks.text: If neither app fits your workflow, compare the [MacWhisper alternatives](/alternatives/macwhisper) and the [VoiceInk alternatives](/alternatives/voiceink). Both pages list prices and privacy notes for other Mac apps.

faq.question: Is MacWhisper better than VoiceInk?
faq.answer: Neither app wins every job. MacWhisper is the better pick for audio and video files, exports and language coverage. VoiceInk suits dictation, public code and one-time licenses for up to three Macs. Test both with the same recording before you pay.

faq.question: Does VoiceInk send my voice to the cloud?
faq.answer: VoiceInk says all voice transcription runs on your device. Its cloud enhancement is optional. If you turn it on, only the transcribed text is processed, not your voice. Check the setting in the app, since a reviewer warned that local is not automatic.

faq.question: Does MacWhisper send my files to the cloud?
faq.answer: MacWhisper says its local models handle sensitive files on your Mac, and cloud AI is optional. Its site does not say where data goes when cloud AI is on. Keep cloud AI off for sensitive work until the vendor explains its data handling.

faq.question: How much does MacWhisper Pro cost?
faq.answer: MacWhisper's site lists Pro as Pay Once at €64 per license, with lifetime updates. The Free tier is €0 and free forever. Check the checkout page for the price in your own currency, since third-party reviews quote other figures.

faq.question: How much does VoiceInk cost?
faq.answer: VoiceInk lists Solo at $25 for one Mac, Personal at $39 for up to two Macs, and Extended at $49 for up to three Macs. Each is a one-time payment with no subscription. The page offers a 14-day money-back guarantee.

faq.question: Does VoiceInk run on Intel Macs?
faq.answer: No. VoiceInk's homepage and pricing page say it works only on Apple silicon Macs. It also requires macOS 14.4 or later and recommends 8GB of RAM.

faq.question: Can Lazur replace MacWhisper or VoiceInk?
faq.answer: Only for some tasks. Lazur answers questions about your screen and dictates with fn. It does not list file transcription or export formats, so it does not replace MacWhisper for interviews. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers, so it is not a local-only app.

faq.question: Are there free trials for these apps?
faq.answer: MacWhisper has a Free tier that its site lists as free forever. VoiceInk's homepage has a free trial button, but the length and terms were not stated on the pages checked. Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card, starting when you first open the app.
